items.title: Cop31 live: clock running down on climate talks as deep divisions remain
items.summary:
Few signs of progress since draft deal exposed disagreements over what countries are willing to do stop the planet heating

The main aim of Cop31 appears to be to protect the UN climate negotiating mechanisms than to achieve real progress, the former Colombian minister in charge of this year’s Santa Marta conference has warned.

Irene Veléz Torres oversaw the Santa Marta meeting in April of more than 50 countries pledging to “transition away from fossil fuels”. Under that “coalition of the willing”, countries are producing roadmaps to phase out fossil fuel extraction and use. Eleven countries have now published such plans, including Germany, France, the Netherlands and Ireland.

items.title: They migrated to New York for work. Now they’re fighting to climate-proof it.
items.summary:
Earlier this year, riding his e-bike through New York City’s bustling streets on a sweltering July afternoon, José Yos began to smell smoke. It wasn’t coming from a nearby burning building or a beat-up yellow cab. Instead, the smell came from hundreds of miles away in Canada. Raging wildfires in Quebec had sent a cloud of thick, smoky air toward the city, blanketing it in a strange orange haze. 

It wasn’t the first time Yos, a 40-year-old from Guatemala who delivers food and groceries on apps like DoorDash, had experienced this. In 2023, Canada had its worst wildfire season on record, with around 37 million acres (15 million hectares) of land going up in flames. Wildfire smoke traveled down from Quebec to New York , polluting the air and turning the skies a deep shade of orange . This summer, though, the city was also in the middle of a heat emergency — its second in as many weeks. The temperature was projected to reach close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit that day, and the heat index — the day’s real feel temperature — was supposed to be even higher. 

In response to the extreme weather double whammy, the city had sent cooling vans around the city, opened additional cooling centers and urged New Yorkers to stay home, ideally in air conditioning. But Yos was on the clock. He couldn’t afford to go home or take a real break. He had reserved his hours on Uber Eats a week in advance and was worried that if he took longer than usual to fulfill orders, his in-app rating would go down, putting him at risk of being deactivated. 

Before the enactment of the city’s deactivation…
items.t: They migrated to New York for work. Now they’re fighting to climate-proof it.

items.title: What Congress’ bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you
items.summary:
The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in Arizona and California, faced opposition from birders, the military, and tribes. While some disputes were resolved, tribes’ concerns about the project’s impacts on historic sites have remained unsettled, leading to court battles that still haven’t been resolved even though the line was completed in June.

Such legal challenges commonly delay renewable energy projects and the transmission lines that carry their power to population centers. The threat of lawsuits and resistance from utilities have driven down long-distance power line construction in the United States, limiting the country’s ability to use cheap renewable energy.

The Senate is poised to pass a “permitting reform” bill that could make it much faster and easier to build transmission lines and renewable energy projects — but it casts a wide net, easing construction for almost all large infrastructure projects. Supporters of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , or BAAJA — including clean energy companies and prominent climate-conscious senators — argue the bill is necessary to clean up the power grid. Critics say it could disempower communities, tribes, and environmental groups while also speeding construction of fossil fuel infrastructure. Once through the Senate, the bill would still need to pass the House and receive the president’s signature before becoming law.…
items.t: What Congress’ bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you

items.title: In Utah, a ‘hydrocarbon highway’ could run right through this petroglyph-filled canyon
items.summary:
Federal land managers call it “the world’s longest art gallery,” a Utah red-rock canyon full of ancient petroglyphs, Native American panels, and Pioneer-era inscriptions written in axle grease. Earlier this year, the Trump administration approved plans to blast a “ hydrocarbon highway ” connecting nearby oil fields to rail-loading facilities through Nine Mile Canyon’s cultural and archaeological-rich sites. Last month environmental and historic preservation groups sued to stop them.

“It’s like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum,” said J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, in a statement.

The Trump administration resurrected the project in eastern Utah after it stalled out during President Joe Biden’s term. Plaintiffs in the lawsuit say approvals for the highway bypassed the normal public comment and ecological review processes. The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and the Center for Biological Diversity filed their complaint in Utah’s U.S. District Court against the Department of Interior and Bureau of Land Management.

Nine Mile Canyon runs about 46 miles. Plans call for dynamiting, paving, and widening a road through Gate Canyon, a tributary to Nine Mile, which has 47 historic sites of its own with 43 eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, according to BLM documentation from 2015.

The proposed highway would cut through 5.3 miles of land owned by both the Bureau of Land Management and Utah’s Trust Lands Administration, although most of the switchbacks the highway project would…
items.t: In Utah, a ‘hydrocarbon highway’ could run right through this petroglyph-filled canyon

items.title: ‘Aarigaa!’: the triumph of Mary Peltola’s historic US Senate win and what it means for Alaska Natives
items.summary:

Late into the night on 3 November, while the lower 48 states were reeling from the blue wave crashing across the US, Mary Peltola took to the stage in a Sheraton Hotel ballroom in Anchorage, Alaska, to greet her supporters.

It wasn’t a victory speech as such – there would still be long days ahead before all votes could be counted across this vast arctic state. But that didn’t prevent the Democratic Senate candidate from expressing her elation, bouncing up and down on stage, clapping her hands and clicking her fingers.

items.title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
items.summary:
Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law

The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.

Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.

items.title: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects
items.summary:
After years of negotiation, Congress is on the cusp of passing a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would make it far easier to build power plants and electric transmission lines in the United States. The bill was negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators including Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse, a noted climate hawk, and Republican Mike Lee, an opponent of environmental regulation. It has picked up support from clean energy advocates because it would promote more transmission lines to carry renewable power to cities, speed up review for solar and wind projects, and stop presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms. It has also been endorsed by many conservative , business , and fossil fuel groups, who say it would cut down on environmental red tape and speed up natural gas pipelines.

The bill has divided the climate movement , separating groups focused on decarbonization from those focused on endangered species protection and environmental justice, but the most influential opposition has come from tribal nations. The bill would weaken a historic preservation law that tribes often use to protect cultural and religious sites from development, and numerous prominent Indigenous nations and organizations have said it harms tribal sovereignty.

While the bill cleared a procedural hurdle in the Senate last week, it remains unclear whether it will pass there or in the House. The negotiators who framed the bill say they believe they have the votes , but a number of Democrats in both chambers have opposed the bill. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has…
items.t: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects

items.title: Nitrates in drinking water are a ‘public health crisis,’ environmentalists warn
items.summary:
When the federal government set its limit on how much nitrate drinking water can safely contain, the primary concern was blue baby syndrome, a condition that deprives infants of oxygen. In the 51 years since then, research has associated exposure to the contaminant with cancer and other health problems, fueling calls for a stricter standard.

On Monday, a coalition of national and local advocacy organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Union of Concerned Scientists, Prairie Rivers Network, and 11 others filed a petition calling on the U.S Environmental Protection Agency to lower that threshold from 10 milligrams per liter to 1 mg/liter. In its petition, the coalition argued that “nitrates in drinking water are causing a public health crisis across the country.” 

“One in three Americans — nearly 120 million people in this country — are currently being served water with dangerous levels of nitrate in it,” said Tyler Lobdell, a senior staff attorney at Food & Water Watch. That figure includes people served water with nitrate concentrations above 1 mg/L — one-tenth of the current federal standard.

Nitrate pollution, much of it linked to fertilizer and manure runoff and leaching from agriculture, is a particular concern in farming regions, where contaminated groundwater can disproportionately impact rural, low-income, Latino , and farmworker communities. Studies have linked exposure with colorectal cancer, thyroid disease, and fetal abnormalities. A 2019 study estimated that up to 12,594 new cancer cases each year are attributable to nitrate in drinking…
items.t: Nitrates in drinking water are a ‘public health crisis,’ environmentalists warn

items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
items.summary:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

items.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
items.summary:
Print article 

Share 

Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.

Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew , a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO .

It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.

Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – have are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.

There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.

Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions , the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.

items.title: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
items.summary:
Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain.

Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer.

Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons .

Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place.

Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity,…
items.t: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

items.t: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?

items.title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
items.summary:
On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state .

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology , while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission , which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this Exxon Mobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working-class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,”…
items.t: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks

Poaching, trafficking, insurgencies and traditional medicine all threaten the central African primates, but a rehabilitation centre offers a haven in Cameroon

Every morning in central Cameroon, the primatologist Sheri Speede wakes to a daunting task. At the Sanaga-Yong sanctuary, which she founded in 1999, there are 75 chimpanzees to feed four times a day and monitor for physical or behavioural issues.

Of those, more than 30 need to be given routine birth-control medications, four are babies requiring round-the-clock care, and two are rowdy teenagers currently being integrated into new social groups.

items.title: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
items.summary:
Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years. 

This one felt different. 

Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.

A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests, and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.

Ruben Juarez, left, and Alika Maunakea are professors at the University of Hawaiʻi and co-leads of the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study.
 Keerti Gopal 

On August 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents, and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt. 

Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health. 

Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of…
items.t: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal

items.title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
items.summary:
The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest , with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations. 

This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.

“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”

Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide $1.8 billion in funding , and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. 

Despite those pledges, funds have been slow to reach affected communities and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and lives remain under constant threat . Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate…
items.t: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
